clue.text: Criminal slain in North Arabian desert — we are all in it together

definitions.text: we are all in it together

parts.note: an Omani is an Arabian from Oman

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are set inside the desert word

parts.note: sand is what a desert is made of

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the letters of the word slain are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A killer has been released into the empty Arabian desert, and the clue moralises that we all share responsibility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' is the anagram signal; the scrambled letters sit inside the desert word, just after its first letter. The answer is John Donne's famous line.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne's line says no person is isolated; everyone is bound up in humanity, which the definition paraphrases.

clue.text: Where informal expressions found to align with Syrian code, oddly translated

indicators.note: translating turns words into a different form, so these letters are rearranged
the odd-numbered letters, first and third, are taken from the word code

explanation.surface: Someone is trying to match a Syrian cipher to some text, with a clumsy translation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' takes CD from 'code'; with TO, ALIGN and SYRIAN those letters are 'translated' into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A reference book listing colloquial terms is where casual, informal phrases are recorded and explained.

clue.text: Stick all fingers and thumbs right into sponge cake

parts.note: a bat is a stick used in games such as cricket
eight fingers plus two thumbs come to ten

indicators.note: the letter for right goes inside the word for sponge

parts.note: to sponge is to cadge or beg

explanation.surface: A clumsy baker pokes a stick into a sponge cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all fingers and thumbs' looks like clumsiness but counts digits. 'Sponge' looks like part of the definition but is the verb BEG; Battenberg is a British chequered sponge cake wrapped in marzipan.
explanation.definitionFit: Battenberg is a specific British confection with pink and yellow squares, so it is an example of a cake.

clue.text: Setter throwing up egg and a piece of chicken

indicators.note: in a down clue, throwing something up flips it so it reads from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a nit is the egg of a louse
a leg is a cut of chicken

explanation.surface: The crossword setter is being sick after eating egg and chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' looks like the crossword compiler, but it is something that makes jellies set. 'throwing up' reverses NIT A LEG.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelatin is the gelling agent added to jellies and desserts to make them firm.

clue.text: Double first's ultimate achievement

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so the final letter of the word first is taken

parts.note: a win is an achievement or success

explanation.surface: A first-ever double is someone's ultimate achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first's ultimate' is the last letter of 'first'.
explanation.definitionFit: A twin is a person or thing that is an exact counterpart, the same as a double or lookalike.

clue.text: Wind blows at 3mph — that should be a breeze

indicators.note: to wind is to twist or coil, so these letters are wound into a new order

parts.note: the digit 3 is written out as the word three
taken as its letters, the abbreviation for miles per hour

explanation.surface: A weather report: a wind blowing at three miles an hour is only a light breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' looks like the weather but is the anagram signal, rearranging BLOWSAT plus THREE and MPH.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something should be easy implies there is no difficulty, which the casual question asks.

clue.text: Figure meat and grain eaten by King Edward, say, part of English course

indicators.note: the three foods are swallowed inside the potato word

parts.note: King Edward is a British potato variety, and tater is slang for potato
ten is a figure, a number
ham is a meat
corn is a grain

explanation.surface: A king eats a meal of meat and grain.
explanation.walkthrough: King Edward is not a monarch but a popular British potato, so TATER. Tattenham Corner is the famous bend on Epsom Downs racecourse, home of the Derby.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattenham Corner is the sharp bend at Epsom Downs racecourse in Surrey, so it is one portion of an English racing track.

clue.text: Oxygen coming in a little lower, excellent source of fuel

indicators.note: the oxygen symbol enters the young animal word

parts.note: a lower is a cow (it lows, or moos), so a little one is a calf
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
ace means excellent

explanation.surface: Something about oxygen levels dropping a little, praised as a fuel source.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lower' reads as 'more low' but is one that lows: a cow.
explanation.definitionFit: The coalface is the exposed seam in a mine where coal is cut, so it is where that fuel comes from.

clue.text: Muted sound when treacherous fascist backed

indicators.note: backed means turned backwards, so the traitor's nickname is read in reverse

parts.note: Lord Haw-Haw was the nickname of William Joyce, who broadcast Nazi propaganda to Britain in the Second World War

explanation.surface: A sound was suppressed when a traitorous fascist was supported.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Haw-Haw was the nickname of the wartime Nazi broadcaster William Joyce, hanged for treason.
explanation.definitionFit: A wah-wah is the wavering effect produced by moving a mute in a trumpet's bell, or a guitar pedal imitating it.

clue.text: Flying pig?

parts.note: a greedy eater is a pig, and the greedy one that flies is a seabird whose name is also used for a glutton

explanation.surface: The proverbial impossibility, a pig that flies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pigs might fly' suggests the impossible, but here the pig is a glutton and the flier a seabird famous for gobbling fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The seabird's name is slang for a greedy person, so a glutton that can fly fits it.

clue.text: Comment on article not finished off

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
to finish off food is to eat it all, so ate

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on a newspaper article that was never completed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finished off' looks like it trims a word, but it is the verb ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To annotate is to add explanatory notes or remarks to a text.

clue.text: Might one be looking up a Spoonerism for Mrs Malaprop?

indicators.note: a Spoonerism swaps the opening sounds of two words, here of a phrase describing the character

parts.note: Mrs Malaprop, in Sheridan's play The Rivals, misuses words, so she is a word botcher; Mrs supplies the first word
her name, from French mal a propos, stands for the second word, one who botches or bungles

explanation.surface: A playful question about whether Sheridan's word-mangling character is gazing upwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the first sounds of WORD BOTCHER gives a phrase that sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A birder spends time scanning trees and skies, so is someone gazing upwards.

clue.text: Arresting boxing scrap, very exciting

indicators.note: boxing means enclosing, so the arresting word goes around the scrap word

parts.note: nailing someone is catching or arresting them
a bit is a scrap or small piece

explanation.surface: An arresting boxing fight, very exciting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boxing scrap' reads as a fight in the ring, but 'boxing' is the container signal and 'scrap' a small piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nail-biting is so tense that spectators gnaw their nails, meaning thrilling.

clue.text: Borrow cooler jacket

parts.note: to bum is slang for to cadge or borrow
a freezer is something that cools

explanation.surface: Someone borrows a cooler jacket for warm weather.
explanation.walkthrough: A bum-freezer is British slang for a short jacket ending at the waist; bum is British slang for the buttocks.
explanation.definitionFit: The short waist-length coat is jokingly named because it leaves the wearer's rear exposed to the cold.

clue.text: See 12
Second US president back in A&E — cause of dysentery?

indicators.note: the second and president pieces go inside the hospital department letters

parts.note: A&E is the British accident and emergency department; its letters are taken
mo is short for moment, a second

indicators.note: back means the president's name is read in reverse

parts.note: Abe is the short name of Abraham Lincoln, the US president

explanation.surface: Lincoln turns up in hospital casualty, perhaps with dysentery.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E is the British hospital emergency department. 'back' reverses the president's name. The question mark warns that this names one example of a cause, amoebic dysentery.
explanation.definitionFit: Amoebic dysentery is caused by single-celled organisms infecting the gut, so these organisms produce it.

clue.text: Stop drug, nothing injected

indicators.note: the nothing letter is injected into the drug word

parts.note: a statin is a cholesterol-lowering drug
O is the round figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: An instruction to stop a drug, with nothing injected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'injected' sounds medical, matching 'drug', but it puts O inside STATIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A station is a regular stopping place for trains or buses.

clue.text: Potential success is in doughnuts or fried onions with salt

indicators.note: the word is goes inside the word for those round snacks

parts.note: both can come as rings: ring doughnuts and onion rings
a salt is an old sailor, also called a tar

explanation.surface: A recipe of doughnuts, fried onions and salt sounds like a promising future.
explanation.walkthrough: 'salt' looks like the seasoning but is a sailor, TAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A promising newcomer tipped for fame is someone likely to succeed in future.

clue.text: Fish stick bought at seaside

definitions.meaning: ... is a name for several fish, such as ... salmon sold in British chip shops
the hard sugary stick sold at British seaside resorts, often with the town's name running through it

explanation.surface: A seaside shopping trip for fish and a stick of candy.
explanation.walkthrough: Seaside rock is a British sweet, a hard cylindrical candy stick with lettering inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock is both a fish name in British fishmongers' trade and the hard sweet stick sold at resorts.

clue.text: Container for flowers, little one filled with primroses initially on plot

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another follows it

parts.note: a plot is a plan or scheme

indicators.note: the toddler word is filled with the initial letter

parts.note: a tot is a small child

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of primroses is taken

explanation.surface: A gardener's container of primroses for a garden plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plot' looks like a patch of garden but is a scheme, PLAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant pot is the vessel in which flowers or seedlings are grown.

clue.text: Cat rolling up in the early hours, awake

indicators.note: in a down clue, rolling up turns the letters so they read from the bottom

parts.note: AM marks the hours after midnight, in the morning
to be up is to be awake

explanation.surface: A cat arrives home in the small hours, still awake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rolling up' reads as arriving, but it reverses AMUP.
explanation.definitionFit: The puma, or cougar, is a large wild feline of the Americas.

clue.text: Sept, Nov: Dec remains

wordplay.reading: SEPT, NOV, DEC: three months each short of its ending

parts.note: three month names, each shown with the same five-letter ending missing; the plural of what is cut off is the answer

explanation.surface: A dated list, September and November leading to December, as if noting what is left of the year.
explanation.walkthrough: Each month ends in EMBER; take those off (plural, since there are several) and SEPT, NOV and DEC are what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Embers are the glowing remnants of a fire once the flames die down.

clue.text: County boundary approached by member of colony

indicators.note: the boundary word is approached, so preceded, by the insect word

parts.note: ants live in colonies
a rim is an edge or boundary

explanation.surface: A colonist approaches a county boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: Antrim is a county of Northern Ireland. 'colony' suggests settlers, but the member is an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Antrim is one of the six traditional counties of Northern Ireland.

clue.text: One with deep ground in which body finally buried, watchful

indicators.note: in which marks the rearranged letters as the container for the next piece
buried means the final letter is put down inside the jumbled letters
ground is crushed, as coffee is, so the letters are mixed up
finally means the last letter of body is taken

explanation.surface: A gravedigger with a deep pit buries a body, keeping a close watch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' looks like earth but is the anagram signal, making OPENEED; 'in which ... buried' puts the last letter of 'body' inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Being alert and vigilant means keeping your eyes wide and fully attentive.
